articleTitle: Smart Grids - the future or fantasy?
publicationTitle: 2009 IET Smart Metering - Making It Happen
abstract: Smart Grids is a common denominator for a wide range of developments that make medium and low voltage grids more intelligent and flexible than they are nowadays. Main motive for Smart Grid initiatives is that such developments improve reliability of supply and/or support the trend towards a more sustainable energy supply. At this moment, medium and low voltage networks can not be remotely observed and controlled. Various companies are developing technologies aiming at creating smarter networks. However, these developments tend to root in technological possibilities, rather than in a sound problem analysis and a structured approach towards its solution. In the recent past, a great variety of sensors, protocols, communication equipment and the like has been designed to support the move towards Smart Grids. However, many of them have not found wide application, which can be at least partly attributed to the fact that there were no "problems" for which they provided a solution so that it was not possible to draw up a positive business case. In summary, there was too much technology push and too little market pull. The fact that some of manufacturers of unsuccessful technologies even blame network operators as conservative instead of improving the price performance ratio of their products further hampers a real take off of Smart Grids. Notwithstanding the mixed present picture, Enexis has high expectations of the future of Smart Grid technologies. In the short term, Enexis focuses on applying Smart Grid technologies for improving the reliability of supply through increasing the speed of restoration after an interruption. To this end, Enexis has planned the large-scale deployment of remote control on certain points in the medium voltage networks to detect and localize outages due to component failures. This makes it no longer necessary to rely on phone calls of people whose lights and televisions turn off for outage detection and makes fault location much quicker. Smart Grid technologies can thus battle the expected increase in component failures, the inevitable consequences of an ageing infrastructure. In the longer term, Smart Grid technologies will play an important role in maintaining reliability of supply and improving sustainability. The complexity of electricity distribution increases. Gardeners connect CHP plants to the grids and the number of wind turbines increases. This also applies for small generators, such as micro CHP plants and PV panels. Smart Grids support these developments by continuously monitoring and controlling the grid and the generators. Enexis believes that effective deployment of Smart Grid technologies requires a top down approach. Therefore Enexis is developing a vision on the role of the medium and low voltage networks in a sustainable energy future. With Enexis' vision becoming clearer over time, ever greater efforts will be spent on developing the appropriate and necessary Smart Grid technologies in cooperation with commercial energy companies, other grid operators and suppliers, as well as to increasingly focused discussions with the regulator and the government on the future energy supply and the role of Smart Grids in it.

articleTitle: Smart metering: The importance of creating a shared vision - start with a clear view of the end game
publicationTitle: 2009 IET Smart Metering - Making It Happen
abstract: In order to achieve maximum return on the often quoted pound7-10 billion investment in smart metering, it is essential that the requirements of the whole energy system, and the main actors within it, are fully considered and optimised for both the medium and long term. The market and operational models that will underpin a national electricity and gas smart meter deployment need to be designed so that they are fit for purpose, flexible and future proofed. They need to take into account current and proposed government legislation, commercial and regulatory drivers on retailers, network operators and primary producers and the drive by Customers for improved service and enhanced product offerings. Given the wide and diverse nature of the outputs required by each of the actors from the deployment of a national smart metering system it is essential that a shared vision is developed for our energy future that will clearly articulate our aims, and guide our design decisions in the next 2-3 years and our deployment decisions in the subsequent 10 years. This could be achieved by the establishment of a Smart Metering Strategic Design Council to not only formulate a shared vision but develop a roadmap and subsequently act as a guiding coalition for an open and transparent central delivery programme. The central delivery programme will then become the mechanism to fully define the overall objectives, design the detail of the market and operational models, detail functional requirements, refine the business case, ensure stakeholder engagement and coordination etc. This will be essential to ensure the optimum solution is identified and maximum return on investment is delivered. The overall objectives should be to achieve: a.) A well functioning and joined up energy supply chain that customers have confidence in b.) A well informed, engaged and empowered population c.) A basis for the support of coherent government and regulatory energy policy. The strategic direction we take, collectively, in the next 2-3 years will shape our industry for at least the next 10-15 years - the choice is ours!

articleTitle: Realising the benefits of smart metering: Creating consumer engagement
publicationTitle: 2009 IET Smart Metering - Making It Happen
abstract: The UK is facing a gap between our peak demands and our generating capacity which, by 2015, makes the possibility of blackouts very real. This paper looks at the impact of that gap on the UK economy, the role that the consumer can play in bridging the gap through adopting more intelligent consumption behaviour, the experience of creating consumer engagement in Sweden and the opportunity for suppliers to transform their relationship with their customers. The twin challenges of climate change and delivering energy security are fundamentally changing the drivers and demands on the sector. These are not just political or regulatory challenges; they are creating socio-economic pressure for new approaches to how our energy needs are satisfied. For consumers, the need to shift perception from controlling their energy bill through the unit rate will shift from focusing on how much they pay per kilowatt hour they consume, to how and when they use energy. More importantly in the context of addressing the energy gap, will be how they can be rewarded for this behavioural change and maintain their motivation to act over the long term. The challenge for suppliers will become how they segment their customer base, develop and market propositions that address the needs of those customers and, most important their ability to identify and target these propositions to those customers that will buy them. The introduction of smart meters or more precisely the information and communication infrastructure that it creates is critical to this transformation.

publicationTitle: 2009 IET Smart Metering - Making It Happen
abstract: There is limited GB information about how much customers will reduce energy use or change behaviour if they get better information. To get the needed information is one of the purpose of the Energy Demand Research Project. This presentation provides an overview of the Energy Demand Research Project. It will also provide an update on the progress of the trials to date.

articleTitle: Smart metering interoperability in the GB market
publicationTitle: 2009 IET Smart Metering - Making It Happen
abstract: Interoperability is a key assumption in the development of smart metering in GB to facilitate the competitive energy retail market. There are 2 elements to interoperability: technical and commercial technical interoperability is largely about defining: functionality of the gas and electricity metering systems interfaces in the provision of smart metering services (format and data content) service requirements of those interfaces. This is deliberately focused on service requirements and interface definitions, rather than existing solutions - these can be assessed once an RFI is out for the services. The definition of technical interoperability will depend on the market model and be driven by the use cases for smart metering. WAN communications interface and local communications interface will be explored. Consumer engagement essential to deliver consumer benefits identified in CBA. Use cases will have to be forward looking to ensure that opportunities such as Demand Side Management and Smart Grids are not precluded by any solution. Commercial Interoperability is every bit as important, as any framework for the operation of smart metering must work commercially and contractual arrangements must be practical (e.g. for single fuel supplies as well as dual fuel supplies). Implications of different market models will be explored. Implementing an operational framework for smart metering is just the beginning. Smart metering itself is just the facilitator - it is what industry does with the smart metering framework that is key to achieving the benefits in the CBA (e.g. flexible tariffs, PAYG offerings, customer behavioural change). There must be a strategic vision for the operation of smart metering. If we need to compromise that vision for day 1 operations, then that is acceptable as long as the long-term vision is not lost and is the target for a series of tactical industry changes to achieve it. We need a Government/Ofgem/industry programme of work to achieve day 1 operation and to set out the strategic target. We must provide a framework for industry efficiencies (see principles and requirements).

publicationTitle: 2009 IET Smart Metering - Making It Happen
abstract: • Energy efficiency has improved substantially since the 1970s but demand continues to grow • To reduce emissions we need to reduce demand as well as fit more energy saving measures • Smart meters could have an important role to play in demand reduction but we need to identify how to get a sustained rather than just a short term response • Smart meters could also deliver new consumer services - e.g. tariffs, better prepay • However, there will be a need for some new consumer protection measures and targeted information, advice and education. • Costs to consumers should be minimised - and benefits achieved.

abstract: This presentation introduces the communications requirements for Smart Metering systems in the UK: • LAN communications within the home for metering (gas and electricity) and home automation (display and appliances) purposes. • WAN communications from the home to head-end computer systems at the energy supplier. These may be direct communications or via street-level data concentrators.

publicationTitle: 2009 IET Smart Metering - Making It Happen
abstract: The speaker explains the experience gained in rolling out an AMR project across the island of Guernsey. The challenges faced include choosing the appropriate technology, choosing the right people to carry out the design, implementation and commissioning of the system and integrating it into many of Guernsey Electricity's primary business systems. Good public relations through local media outlets ensured that customers embraced the changes and the project has been a resounding success so far…
